Case study 01 · PrepLadder · Data governance · KPI design · Dashboarding

Revenue Intelligence Center

Creating one governed view of revenue, leads and sales performance. I brought lead and revenue reporting onto shared data rules, connecting three source datasets to eight reporting views. A recorded snapshot covered 30,493 lead rows and 49,965 revenue rows.

Recorded30,493lead rows in the snapshot
Recorded49,965revenue rows in the snapshot
Calculated80,458rows on one rule set
Recorded8reporting views

The problem

Leadership and cluster heads relied on manually shared trackers with mixed formats, broken headers and inconsistent ownership. Different definitions could produce different answers to the same business question.

Objective

Create a common data foundation and a set of role-specific reporting views driven by shared mappings and business rules.

Process

  1. Map decisionsList the questions leaders and field teams need answered: overview, inputs, outputs, SA, territory, visits, portfolio and comparison.
  2. Govern source dataSeparate lead data, revenue data and SA/college master data, with one shared mapping layer.
  3. Profile and validateInspect headers, missing values, ownership and mapping inconsistencies before calculating metrics.
  4. Apply business rulesCalculate KPIs from governed inputs rather than redefining logic in each dashboard.
  5. Deliver viewsPresent a shared overview plus operational and management views.
Portal exports→Lead + revenue + master data→Profile / clean / validate→Shared mapping + rules→KPI layer→8 dashboard views

Results and evidence

  • 30,493 lead rows and 49,965 revenue rows were recorded under the shared rule set (80,458 combined, calculated).
  • Three source-of-truth datasets: leads, revenue, and SA/college master data.
  • Eight views: overview, inputs, outputs, SA, territory, visits, portfolio and comparison.
  • A three-way scoreboard (vs last month, vs last year, YTD) and a CH view with targets and incentive context.

Rows under the shared rule set

Source: recorded snapshot of the governed lead and revenue databases.

Visual evidence

Illustrative visuals from my dashboard showcase: not production performance data.

Tools

Google SheetsApps ScriptProfiler script

Limitations and next steps

Counts come from one snapshot, and usage of each view by role is not tracked yet. Next: view-level usage and a data-freshness indicator.

What this demonstrates

Metric definition, data governance, KPI design, requirements translation and stakeholder alignment.

Case study 02 · PrepLadder · Time-series comparison · Variance analysis · Planning support

Performance Review & Planning Support

Comparing like with like, then planning from it. I set up the like-for-like comparisons used in performance reviews and prepared planning inputs for leadership, including a costed BD hiring plan.

Rule3-waycomparison on every review
Rule85%pace threshold for flags
Target₹126 Lhiring plan, presented for approval

The problem

Month-to-date numbers were compared with full past months, so teams looked behind or ahead for the wrong reasons, and targets lacked a common reference.

Objective

Give every review the same comparison frame, flag pacing problems mid-month and turn history into planning inputs leadership can use.

Process

  1. Compare like with likeThis month vs the same days last month, the same days last year, and YTD vs YTD.
  2. Pace the monthCurrent and required run rate with a month-end projection; anyone below 85% of pace is flagged.
  3. Set targetsCluster-head targets built from last year's reference months by product line; pack targets derived from revenue targets with weighted average prices.
  4. Support decisionsPrepared a BD hiring plan for 840 colleges (20 BDMs + 2 CHs, ₹126 L) that was presented to the CEO.
  5. Roll outSupported the calling CRM rollout to BDMs and CHs with rules and instructions.
Revenue + lead history→Same-days comparisons→Run-rate pacing→Reference-month targets→Leadership review

Results and evidence

  • One review format across revenue, packs, AOV, leads, signup % and lead → paid.
  • Pacing flags surface gaps during the month rather than after it.
  • A costed hiring plan (20 BDMs + 2 CHs, ₹126 L) prepared and presented to the CEO; approval status is not claimed here.

This is historical comparison and planning support, not a statistical forecast model.

Visual evidence

Illustrative visuals from my dashboard showcase: not production performance data.

Tools

Google SheetsApps ScriptDaily GM review

Limitations and next steps

Comparisons describe history; they are not a forecast model. Next: a simple forecast with a stated error measure.

What this demonstrates

Time-series and variance analysis, target setting, executive communication and change enablement.

Case study 03 · PrepLadder · Funnel analysis · Cohort definition

Lead → Sign-up → Payment Funnel

Separating lead volume from actual conversion. I separated lead volume from downstream outcomes using a defined lead → valid sign-up → paid-user funnel. One historical cohort had 7,800 leads and 316 paid users: a calculated lead-to-paid rate of 4.05%.

Calculated20.94%lead → valid sign-up (1,633 / 7,800)
Calculated19.35%valid sign-up → paid (316 / 1,633)
Calculated4.05%lead → paid (316 / 7,800)

The problem

Lead volume alone can make acquisition look healthier than it is. A consistent funnel needs explicit definitions for leads, valid sign-ups and paid users.

Objective

Define event windows and measure conversion between each stage so drop-offs become questions to investigate.

Process

  1. Define stagesSeparate leads, valid sign-ups and paid users.
  2. Set event windowsA valid sign-up happens on the scan date (an earlier version allowed up to 3 days); paid means payment in the sign-up month.
  3. Count consistentlyApply the same cohort and date rules to each stage.
  4. Calculate conversionMeasure stage-to-stage and end-to-end conversion.
  5. Investigate drop-offExplore lead quality, contactability, follow-up and sign-up/payment friction, without assuming a cause from counts alone.
Lead (scan month)→Valid sign-up→Paid in sign-up month→Stage conversion

Results and evidence

  • Lead → valid sign-up: 1,633 / 7,800 = 20.94% (calculated).
  • Valid sign-up → paid: 316 / 1,633 = 19.35% (calculated).
  • Lead → paid: 316 / 7,800 = 4.05% (calculated).
  • 6,167 leads did not reach a valid sign-up and 1,317 valid sign-ups did not pay; these gaps show where to look, not why users dropped out.

One historical cohort: lead → valid sign-up → paid

Counts recorded for one cohort; percentages calculated. Definitions in step 02.

Visual evidence

Illustrative visuals from my dashboard showcase: not production performance data.

Tools

Google SheetsCohort rules

Limitations and next steps

Counts show where users drop, not why. Next: test causes such as contactability and follow-up speed.

What this demonstrates

Funnel analysis, cohort definition, conversion measurement, hypothesis generation and clear metric communication.

Case study 04 · PrepLadder · Workflow automation · Data validation

Reporting Factory

Turning recurring sales reporting into a repeatable pipeline. I redesigned recurring sales reporting as a repeatable pipeline, from portal export and validation to KPI calculation and distribution, removing an estimated 30 minutes of manual work per hourly cycle.

Estimate~30 minmanual work removed per hourly cycle
Recorded50+BDMs, plus 10 CHs and leadership, receive it

The problem

Recurring reports required repeated exports, cleanup, tracker updates, formatting and distribution. Repeating these steps every cycle creates delay and inconsistent outputs.

Objective

Structure reporting as a controlled pipeline: extract, validate, calculate, publish and distribute.

Process

  1. ExtractDownload the relevant sales-portal CSV for the reporting period.
  2. PrepareLoad the export into the raw-data sheet while preserving business meaning.
  3. ValidateCheck columns, dates, ownership, missing values and row structure.
  4. CalculateApply shared business rules and feed the KPI layer.
  5. PublishRefresh the tracker or dashboard and distribute the report.
Sales portal→CSV export→Raw data→Clean + validate→KPI layer→Tracker + dashboard→Distribution

Results and evidence

  • About 30 minutes of manual effort removed from each hourly reporting cycle (estimate, not a time study).
  • Audience: 50+ BDMs, 10 CHs and senior sales leadership.
  • Every cycle runs the same steps: extract, validate, apply rules, report, distribute.

Manual minutes per hourly reporting cycle

Estimate from the reporting history, not an audited time study.

Tools

PythonPlaywrightApps ScriptGoogle SheetsTask SchedulerWhatsApp

Limitations and next steps

Time saved is an estimate, not a time study. Next: log run times and failures to measure reliability.

What this demonstrates

Workflow analysis, automation design, operational reliability and stakeholder service.

Case study 05 · PrepLadder · Process controls · Exception handling · Incentive allocation

Incentive & Payout Operations

Making incentive processing more controlled and predictable. I structured incentive processing around validation, eligibility rules, calculation and exception handling. The recorded cycle went from about 10 days to 3 days.

Reported10 → 3 dayspayout cycle
Calculated−70%if the cycles are comparable
Rule0.7 · 0.15 · 0.15scoring weights

The problem

Incentive workflows become slow when eligibility, identity/KYC checks, calculation rules and payout preparation are handled across disconnected manual steps.

Objective

Make the workflow explicit, validate inputs early, apply consistent rules and surface exceptions before payout.

Process

  1. CollectBring participant and incentive details into one structured input.
  2. ValidateCheck required KYC fields and eligibility.
  3. CalculateApply documented incentive rules consistently: 0.7 × revenue + 0.15 × leads + 0.15 × SA activation achievement.
  4. Review exceptionsFlag incomplete or mismatched records instead of passing them through.
  5. Prepare outputProduce a reviewable, payout-ready report for Finance.
Form input→Sheets→KYC + eligibility checks→Rule-based calculation→Exception review→Finance report

Results and evidence

  • Payout cycle recorded at about 10 days before and 3 days after.
  • That is a 7-day (70%) reduction if the two periods are comparable completed cycles (calculated).
  • Validation and consistent calculation are built into the flow; no accuracy improvement is claimed without error data.

Incentive payout cycle

Recorded before/after cycle times; the 70% figure assumes comparable cycles.

Visual evidence

Illustrative visuals from my dashboard showcase: not production performance data.

Tools

Google FormsGoogle SheetsApps ScriptOCR / AI checks

Limitations and next steps

The 10 → 3 day figure compares recorded cycles; no accuracy change is claimed without error data. Next: track exceptions per cycle.

What this demonstrates

Process design, controls, exception management, incentive operations and turnaround-time analysis.

Case study 06 · PrepLadder · CRM governance · Data quality rules · Attribution

Lead Ownership & Calling-Credit Governance

Reducing ambiguity in lead ownership and attribution. I addressed ambiguity in lead ownership and calling attribution by defining one accountable owner per lead and a verifiable calling-credit rule, delivered through a Google Workspace calling CRM. The baseline identified 673 multi-owner leads.

Recorded673multi-owner leads in the baseline
Rule1owner per lead (target state)
Recorded~12Kevent leads a month, 49 BDMs
Recorded~575automated checks before launch

The problem

Multiple owners on one lead weaken follow-up accountability and create disputes about calling credit. ~12,000 event leads a month reached 49 BDMs, and every purchase was being counted as a calling win.

Objective

One accountable owner per lead and a verifiable rule for calling credit, with exceptions visible.

Process

  1. Find conflictsIdentify leads with multiple owners or inconsistent assignment (673 in the baseline).
  2. Define ownershipAlready owned stays owned → SA code resolves to a BDM → learner match → otherwise parked with a reason.
  3. Verify callingCredit only if the BDM dialed, the learner paid after the call, and payment data credits the same BDM.
  4. Audit exceptionsReview records that fail the rule.
  5. Report governed outcomesBDM sheets capture calls; dashboards read a separate hourly read-only dump.
Source leads (12:00)→Processing (12:30)→Private BDM sheets (13:15)→Hourly dump + payment check→Dashboard

Results and evidence

  • 673 leads with two or more owners were identified in the baseline.
  • Target state: one owner per lead; calling credit is verified-only under the stated rule.
  • CRM live for BDMs and CHs from 15 Oct 2026, after 12 offline test suites (~575 checks).

Visual evidence

Slides from my CRM case-study carousel; any data shown is fictional or sample.

Tools

Google SheetsApps ScriptProtected ranges

Limitations and next steps

The 673 baseline is from the first run; a post-launch audit will confirm the resolved count. Next: publish monthly ownership-conflict counts.

What this demonstrates

Data governance, accountability design, incentive control, exception handling and stakeholder alignment.

Case study 07 · PrepLadder · Policy design · Risk controls · SLA design

Pricing & Discount Compliance

Turning commercial rules into an operating process. I formalised pricing and discount compliance into an operating policy with defined reporting, verification and response timelines, approved by the BD Head and HR Head.

Rule2 daysto report a suspected breach
Rule3 daysto verify
Rule2 daysto respond

The problem

When sales channels interpret discounts, offers, coupons and attribution differently, commercial consistency is hard to maintain and exceptions are difficult to resolve. Some ambassadors were advertising their own discounts.

Objective

Make approved rules, reporting timelines and escalation paths clear to BD and SA/ISA teams.

Process

  1. Define scopeDocument the channels and offer/discount behaviours covered.
  2. State permitted rulesOfficial pricing, discounts and exception handling only.
  3. Set review processWho reports, who verifies, and the expected response time.
  4. CommunicateDistribute the approved policy and instructions.
  5. Track complianceUse acknowledgements and violation records to assess adherence.
Suspected breach→Report ≤ 2 working days→Verify ≤ 3 working days→Respond ≤ 2 working days→Graded action

Results and evidence

  • Policy timelines: report within 2 working days, verify within 3, respond within 2.
  • Graded breach levels with a show-cause step before any action.
  • These are policy timelines; no measured reduction in violations is claimed yet.

Policy response timeline

Policy timelines, not measured SLA performance.

Tools

Policy draftingGoogle SheetsApps ScriptGmail

Limitations and next steps

Timelines are policy, not measured SLA performance. Next: track acknowledgements and verified breaches.

What this demonstrates

Policy design, risk controls, commercial governance, communication and escalation design.

Case study 08 · PrepLadder · Field operations · Coverage tracking

Exam-Centre Campaign Operations

Coordinating field execution, lead capture and follow-up. I structured exam-centre operations around coverage, clear field ownership, lead capture and follow-up visibility. Snapshots include a NEET PG operation with about 60 BDMs and 10 CHs, plus an FMGE coverage update.

Recorded~60BDMs in the NEET PG operation
Calculated21 / 46FMGE centres filled at one snapshot
Target200leads per centre (target)

The problem

Offline exam-centre campaigns need coordinated coverage, clear field responsibilities, structured lead capture and timely follow-up across many locations.

Objective

Connect centre planning, BDM ownership, lead capture, follow-up and campaign reporting in one operating process.

Process

  1. Map coverageList target centres and identify assigned or unfilled locations.
  2. Assign ownershipMake responsibilities and pending confirmations visible.
  3. Capture leadsAssigned QR forms or paper sheets, uploaded by 8 PM, with geo-tagged photos for reimbursement.
  4. Track follow-upDistribute captured leads into the calling CRM and monitor next actions.
  5. Review executionCompare planned coverage with confirmations, actual activity and valid leads.
Centre list→BDM assignment→QR / sheet capture→Upload by 8 PM→CRM follow-up→Review

Results and evidence

  • NEET PG (30 Aug) operation involved about 60 BDMs and 10 CHs.
  • A target of 200 leads per centre was set; it is a target, not a result.
  • FMGE snapshot: 21 centre commitments filled and 25 confirmations pending at that time.
  • Operational target in the FMGE / INI-CET field manual: 100+ genuine leads per BDM per day (a target, not a result).

Case study 09 · PrepLadder · Master-data reconciliation · Data quality

College Coverage & Data Reconciliation

Making institution coverage and mapping gaps visible. I designed a reconciliation approach that compares the internal college master with a reference list, classifies matches and gaps, and turns data-quality issues into a reviewable coverage list.

Rule4match classes: matched, internal-only, reference-only, duplicate

The problem

College lists and sales coverage data differ in naming and completeness. Without reconciliation, teams can miss institutions or misread coverage.

Objective

Create a comparable institution list and make mismatches, duplicates and coverage gaps explicit.

Process

  1. Standardise namesNormalise spelling, spacing and naming variations.
  2. Match listsCompare the internal college master with a reference list.
  3. ClassifySeparate matches, internal-only, reference-only and possible duplicates.
  4. Summarise coverageCalculate totals and coverage rates from reconciled records.
  5. Route gapsCreate a review list for manual confirmation and follow-up.
Internal master→Reference list→Normalise names→Match + classify→Coverage summary→Review list

Results and evidence

  • The design exposes matched records, missing records and overall coverage.
  • Status: designed and in progress; final reconciled counts are not published yet.

Tools

Google SheetsCOUNTIF / FILTER logic

Limitations and next steps

In progress; final reconciled counts are not available yet.

What this demonstrates

Data quality, master-data management, reconciliation, territory analysis and exception triage.
